analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals, nursing homes, and care employers to write and enforce plans to prevent violence against their workers.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat untouched in three House committees since its April 2025 introduction, with no hearing or vote, despite 134 bipartisan cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would order the Labor Department to write a binding workplace-safety rule for the health care and social service sectors. Covered employers — hospitals, nursing homes, psychiatric facilities, home health agencies, ambulance services, and similar settings — would have to create a written violence-prevention plan with employee input, investigate every violent incident, train workers annually, keep a log of violent incidents for five years, and report yearly totals to the government. Hospitals and nursing homes not already covered by federal or state safety law would have to comply to keep taking Medicare money.
analysis.who_benefits: Health care and social service workers — nurses, aides, psychiatric staff, social workers, home health visitors, and emergency responders — who the bill covers at hospitals, nursing homes, group homes, correctional clinics, and in the field [S3]. The bill gives them a legally enforceable say in safety planning, a right to report hazards without retaliation, and access to their employer's incident records [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nurses, aides, social workers, and EMTs

how_it_helps.text: Every covered employer must develop and maintain a written workplace violence prevention plan, tailored to each facility, with the participation of direct-care employees and their representatives [S3].
Employers must promptly investigate every violent incident or reported hazard, document corrective measures, and maintain a violent-incident log and five-year records that employees can examine [S3].

Workers get annual, in-person, language-appropriate training on hazards, response procedures, and their rights, plus an anti-retaliation policy protecting anyone who reports violence or seeks help from police or regulators [S3].

Employers must use the 'hierarchy of controls' to fix hazards, including engineering measures like alarm systems, weapon detectors, barriers, and enclosed workstations, and staffing practices like adequate numbers of staff and security personnel [S3].
Hospitals and skilled nursing facilities not already covered by the Occupational Safety and Health Act must comply with the standard as a condition of participating in Medicare [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers — hospital systems, nursing homes, home care agencies, staffing firms, and ambulance operators — bear the costs of writing plans, installing controls, training workers annually, investigating incidents, and keeping records. Some of that cost may be passed to patients, insurers, and public health programs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hospitals, nursing homes, and home care operators

drawbacks.text: The bill fast-tracks the safety rule by bypassing the Occupational Safety and Health Act's normal standard-setting process, the Administrative Procedure Act's full rulemaking procedures, the Paperwork Reduction Act, and central regulatory review — allowing only a 30-day public comment period before the interim rule takes effect [S3].

Compliance costs — security hardware, alarm systems, added staffing, annual training, and paperwork — fall on hospitals and nursing homes, some of which operate on thin margins, and could be passed on to patients and public programs [S3].
The bill's coverage is incomplete: it excludes private physician and dentist offices and excludes child day care services, leaving some workers in comparable settings unprotected [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is concrete: workers in settings with some of the highest rates of customer and patient violence would get enforceable prevention plans, incident tracking, and a retaliation shield, on a model OSHA itself published as voluntary guidance in 2015 [S3]. The main costs are administrative and capital, borne by employers; the strongest good-faith objection is procedural — Congress dictating the rule's contents and short-circuiting the usual notice-and-comment safeguards — rather than the safety goal itself. Whether the mandate is well-calibrated depends on how the Labor Department phases in engineering-control requirements, which the bill leaves to the Secretary within limits [S3].

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2025, referred to three House committees the same day, and has seen no hearing, markup, or vote since [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Courtney introduced the bill on April 1, 2025, joined at introduction by Reps. Don Bacon, Robert C. 'Bobby' Scott, Brian Fitzpatrick, Ilhan Omar, and Alma Adams — a bipartisan group of two Republicans and four Democrats [S3].

The same day, it was referred to the Education and Workforce Committee and additionally to Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means, with the Speaker to decide which committee handles which provisions [S5].
134 members have cosponsored it: 129 of 217 House Democrats and 5 of 223 House Republicans [S4].
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action has been scheduled [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, health care and social service employers are better off: no federal violence-prevention standard exists, and no employer faces the bill's plan, training, recordkeeping, or Medicare-condition requirements. Workers in these settings remain covered only by voluntary federal guidance [S3].

for.name: Joe Courtney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a bipartisan group of original cosponsors.

for.name: 5 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Don Bacon (R-NE) and Brian Fitzpatrick (R-PA).

against.name: Tim Walberg
against.role: Chair, House Education and Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill since its referral.

against.name: Brett Guthrie
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled action on the bill, which touches Medicare participation conditions within his committee's jurisdiction.

against.name: Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled action on the bill, which was also referred to his committee.

against.name: Hospital and nursing home industry groups
against.what_they_did: Have historically lobbied against making OSHA's voluntary workplace-violence guidance a binding, enforceable standard for their members.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship is heavily one-sided — 129 of 217 House Democrats versus 5 of 223 House Republicans — though the bill originated with bipartisan sponsorship from two Republicans [S4].

industries.note: They would bear the costs of prevention plans, security controls, training, investigations, and incident records, with Medicare participation as an enforcement lever [S2][S3]. Their interest in avoiding those costs runs against the worker-safety outcome the bill targets.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and long-term care facilities
industries.note: Explicitly covered facilities that would have to comply with the standard, and skilled nursing facilities not under OSHA's jurisdiction would face it as a Medicare condition [S3].
Home health, hospice, and home-based social work are covered services, and contractors, temporary firms, and employee-leasing entities are explicitly covered employers [S3].

industries.industry: Health care and social service workers
industries.note: The bill's whole purpose is to protect them from workplace violence, and their interest in safer conditions runs directly alongside the public's interest in a functioning care system [S3].

analysis.trajectory: Most House bills never get a hearing, and this one has seen none since its April 2025 referral to three committees. With a year and a half left in this Congress, the realistic paths forward are narrow: committee action has not begun, and floor time would likely require either a committee markup that has not been scheduled or attachment to a larger health or labor package. As it stands, the bill is on track to die quietly at the end of this Congress.
